title: Chapter 10 — A Bosom Friend
paragraphs: Returning to the Spouter-Inn from the Chapel, I found Queequeg there quite alone, as he had left the Chapel some time before the benediction. He was sitting on a bench in front of the fire, with his feet on the stove hearth, and in one hand he was holding that little negro idol of his close up to his face, peering hard into its face, and gently whittling away at its nose with a jackknife, meanwhile humming to himself in his heathenish way.

When I interrupted him, he put the idol away. Soon he went to the table, picked up a large book, placed it on his lap, and began counting the pages with careful regularity. At every fiftieth page — as I imagined — he'd stop, look vaguely around, and let out a long, gurgling whistle of astonishment. Then he'd start again at the next fifty, seeming to begin at one each time, as if he couldn't count past fifty — and it was only the sheer number of fifties that amazed him.

I sat watching him with great interest. Savage though he was, and hideously marred about the face — at least to my taste — his face still had something in it that was by no means disagreeable. You cannot hide the soul. Through all his unearthly tattooings, I thought I saw the traces of a simple, honest heart; and in his large, deep eyes, fiery black and bold, there seemed to be signs of a spirit that would dare a thousand devils. And besides all this, there was a certain lofty bearing about the Pagan, which even his uncouthness could not altogether spoil. He looked like a man who had never cringed and never had a creditor. Whether it was also that, his head being shaved, his forehead stood out in freer and brighter relief, and looked broader than it otherwise would, I will not venture to decide; but it was certain that his head was phrenologically an excellent one. It may seem ridiculous, but it reminded me of General Washington's head, as seen in the popular busts of him. It had the same long, regularly graded slope retreating from above the brows, which likewise projected a great deal, like two long promontories thickly wooded on top. Queequeg was George Washington cannibalistically developed.

While I was scanning him so closely, half-pretending all the while to be looking out the window at the storm, he never paid attention to my presence, never bothered himself with so much as a single glance, but seemed wholly occupied with counting the pages of the marvelous book. Considering how sociably we had slept together the night before, and especially considering the affectionate arm I had found thrown over me when I woke in the morning, I thought this indifference of his very strange. But savages are strange beings; at times you do not know exactly how to take them. At first they are overawing; the calm self-collectedness of their simplicity seems a Socratic wisdom. I had also noticed that Queequeg never mixed at all, or only very little, with the other seamen in the inn. He made no advances whatever, and seemed to have no desire to widen his circle of acquaintances. All this struck me as mighty peculiar; yet on second thought there was something almost sublime in it. Here was a man some twenty thousand miles from home — by way of Cape Horn, that is, which was the only way he could get there — thrown among people as strange to him as if he were on the planet Jupiter; and yet he seemed entirely at his ease, keeping the utmost serenity, content with his own company, always equal to himself. Surely this was a touch of fine philosophy, though no doubt he had never heard there was such a thing. But perhaps, to be true philosophers, we mortals should not be conscious of living or striving that way. As soon as I hear that such-and-such a man sets himself up as a philosopher, I conclude that, like the dyspeptic old woman, he must have "broken his digester."

As I sat in that now-lonely room — the fire burning low, in that gentle stage when, having warmed the air, it just glows to be looked at; the evening shadows and phantoms gathering at the windows, peering in at us, a silent, solitary pair; the storm booming outside in solemn swells — I began to feel strange sensations. Something was melting in me. My splintered heart and furious fist were no longer turned against the wolfish world. This soothing savage had redeemed it. There he sat, his very indifference revealing a nature free of civilized hypocrisies and smooth deceits. Wild he was — a sight of sights to see. Yet I began to feel myself mysteriously drawn to him. And the very things that would have repelled most people were the magnets that attracted me. I'll try a pagan friend, I thought, since Christian kindness has proved to be hollow courtesy. I moved my bench closer and made friendly signs and hints, doing my best to talk with him. At first he barely noticed, but when I mentioned his hospitality the night before, he managed to ask whether we'd be bedfellows again. I said yes, and he seemed pleased — perhaps a little flattered.

We turned over the book together, and I tried to explain the purpose of printing and the meaning of the few pictures in it. This caught his interest, and from there we moved on to chattering as best we could about the various sights to see in this famous town. Soon I suggested we smoke together. He produced his pouch and tomahawk-pipe and quietly offered me a puff. And then we sat, exchanging puffs from that wild pipe of his, passing it regularly back and forth.

If any ice of indifference toward me was still hiding in the Pagan's heart, this pleasant, friendly smoke of ours soon melted it and left us pals. He seemed to take to me just as naturally and spontaneously as I did to him; and when we had finished smoking, he pressed his forehead against mine, clasped me around the waist, and told me that from then on we were married — which, in the idiom of his country, meant we were bosom friends; he would gladly die for me if it came to that. In one of my own countrymen, such a sudden flare of friendship would have seemed far too hasty, and much to be distrusted; but those old rules didn't apply to this simple savage.

After supper and another sociable chat and smoke, we went to our room together. He gave me his embalmed head as a present; then he took out his huge tobacco pouch, felt around under the tobacco, and pulled out about thirty dollars in silver. Spreading the coins on the table, he mechanically split them into two equal piles, pushed one toward me, and said it was mine. I was about to object, but he cut me off by pouring them into my trouser pockets. I let them stay there. Then he began his evening prayers, took out his idol, and removed the papered fire-board. From certain signs and hints, I thought he seemed eager for me to join him; but knowing perfectly well what would follow, I considered for a moment whether, if he asked me, I would go along with it or not.

I was a good Christian, born and bred in the bosom of the infallible Presbyterian Church. How then could I join this wild idolator in worshipping his piece of wood? But what is worship? I thought. Do you suppose now, Ishmael, that the magnanimous God of heaven and earth — pagans and all included — can possibly be jealous of an insignificant bit of black wood? Impossible! But what is worship? To do the will of God — that, and nothing else, is worship. And what is the will of God? To do to my fellow man what I would have my fellow man do to me — that, and nothing else, is the will of God. Now, Queequeg is my fellow man. And what do I wish this Queequeg would do to me? Why, join me in my own particular Presbyterian form of worship. Consequently, I must then join him in his; therefore, I must turn idolator. So I lit the shavings; helped prop up the innocent little idol; offered him burnt biscuit with Queequeg; salaamed, bowing low before him, two or three times; kissed his nose; and that done, we undressed and went to bed, at peace with our own consciences and all the world. But we did not go to sleep without a little chat.

How it is, I don't know; but there is no place like a bed for confidential disclosures between friends. Man and wife, they say, open the very bottom of their souls to each other there; and some old couples often lie and chat over old times till nearly morning. So, then, in our hearts' honeymoon, Queequeg and I lay there — a cozy, loving pair.
